neighbours.label: A Korean, Chinese or Japanese character that begins a new word right after a space, mid-sentence (spaced Korean words, Chinese written with spaces between characters, a Korean/Chinese word dropped into an English sentence after a space). The same CJK/Korean text written without spaces is mostly quiet (rare characters can reach about 0.4), as is the first word of a text, and emoji, Thai, Georgian or Cyrillic after a space stay quiet; English words about Korea or China do not fire.
neighbours.short: CJK/Korean character starting a word after a space
fire: She said 감사합니다 to the waiter before leaving.
我 今天 很 高兴 见到 你。
The sign at the door read 欢迎 in large red letters.
My grandmother always calls me 아가 when I visit her.
这 本 书 非常 有意思。
He ordered the 김치 찌개 and a bowl of rice.
quiet: She said thank you to the waiter before leaving.
The sign at the door read welcome in large red letters.
My grandmother always calls me sweetie when I visit her.
He ordered the kimchi stew and a bowl of rice, a classic Korean dish.
neighbours.notes: Test sentences written blind by a second author who saw only the label (blind:claude-opus-5-5 (label-only)). Feeders-first arm: top feeders L32/N4095+ (machine guess: space+byte piece ' �'), L24/N11345+ (same, first appearance), L29/N360+ (CJK byte sequence) shaped the tokenizer-level hypothesis. Little to do with the Dniester feeder; the drop comes from one of its top examples.

predictions: Spaced Korean/Chinese fire sentences beat their unspaced twins; risk: Chinese characters that are whole tokens (no byte split) may stay quiet even when spaced.
